hints: Focus on the reagent condition, NaOH in ethanol with heat means elimination to form alkenes, not substitution to form alcohols.
Start with 1-chlorobutane, it can only lose hydrogen from C2, so it gives only but-1-ene which shows no E/Z isomerism.
Now look at 2-chlorobutane, it can form both but-1-ene and but-2-ene, and remember but-2-ene exists as E and Z forms, so count only unique molecules overall.
walkthrough:
**Spot the reaction type**

Great start, always check the conditions first. Aqueous NaOH gives substitution, but ethanolic NaOH with heat gives elimination of HCl to form an alkene.

Elimination rule:
$$\text{R-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{Cl} + \text{NaOH (ethanol, heat)} \rightarrow \text{alkene} + \text{NaCl} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Eliminate 1-chlorobutane**

1-chlorobutane is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$. The Cl is on C1, so hydrogen can only be removed from the neighbouring C2.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Cl} \rightarrow \text{CH}_2\text{=CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3 + \text{HCl}$$
This is but-1-ene. It has two H atoms on C1 of the double bond, so no E/Z stereoisomerism is possible.

**Eliminate 2-chlorobutane**

2-chlorobutane is $\text{CH}_3\text{CHClCH}_2\text{CH}_3$. The Cl is on C2, so hydrogen can be removed from C1 or from C3. This gives two structural alkenes.

From C1:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CHClCH}_2\text{CH}_3 \rightarrow \text{CH}_2\text{=CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$$
From C3:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CHClCH}_2\text{CH}_3 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH=CHCH}_3$$
But-2-ene has two different groups on each C of the double bond, so it exists as E (trans) and Z (cis) stereoisomers.

**Count unique organic molecules**

Now put it together and do not double count. But-1-ene is made from both starting materials but it is the same molecule, so count it once.

Unique products are: but-1-ene, (E)-but-2-ene, (Z)-but-2-ene. That is 3 different organic molecules in total.

options.A: Not correct. This would mean only one alkene forms in total. It ignores that 2-chlorobutane can eliminate in two directions to give both but-1-ene and but-2-ene.
options.B: Not correct. This counts the two structural alkenes, but-1-ene and but-2-ene, but forgets stereoisomerism. But-2-ene exists as distinct E and Z isomers, so the total is more than 2.
options.C: Correct, well done. 1-chlorobutane gives but-1-ene only. 2-chlorobutane gives but-1-ene plus E-but-2-ene and Z-but-2-ene. Counting unique molecules gives but-1-ene, E-but-2-ene and Z-but-2-ene, which is 3.
options.D: Not correct. This is the common double counting trap. It adds 1 product from 1-chlorobutane plus 3 products from 2-chlorobutane to get 4, but but-1-ene formed from both routes is the same molecule and must be counted only once.
